interview.question: What is Node.js's global WebSocket used for?
interview.answer: The global WebSocket provides a browser-compatible client API for bidirectional communication with a server. It is available without importing a package, and construction immediately begins the opening handshake.
interview.followUp: What URL schemes are accepted? Only ws: and wss: are valid; wss: provides the secure variant.

interview.question: How do you construct a WebSocket and negotiate protocols?
interview.answer: Use new WebSocket(url, protocols?) to create a connection. The second argument can be one subprotocol, an array of subprotocols, or a WebSocketInit object.
interview.followUp: Why might protocols be supplied? They let the client and server negotiate an application-level subprotocol during connection setup.

interview.question: What lifecycle constraint applies after close?
interview.answer: The instance represents one connection and cannot be reused after it closes. To reconnect, construct a new WebSocket with the target URL.
interview.followUp: When does network activity begin? The opening handshake starts immediately during construction, before later event handlers run.

keyPoints: Node.js provides a browser-compatible global WebSocket client.
Each WebSocket object corresponds to one connection.
Instantiation starts the connection handshake immediately.
The API manages a connection that supports server communication.
Communication can flow in both directions between client and server.
The implementation follows the WHATWG WebSocket specification and RFC 6455.
gotchas: The connection URL must use either the ws: or wss: scheme.
A WebSocket instance is single-use after closure; create another instance for a new connection.

Streams & buffers::Backpressure.summary: Writable-stream backpressure is signaled when write() returns false. Stop writing and wait for the stream's drain event before continuing, or queued data can grow without bound.
Streams & buffers::Backpressure.explanation: A writable stream buffers data until its internal queue reaches the highWaterMark. When write() returns false, stop submitting chunks; the stream emits drain after buffered data has been accepted for delivery, signaling that writing may continue.

parameters.name: chunk
parameters.description: Data to write to the stream.

parameters.name: encoding
parameters.description: Character encoding used when chunk is a string.

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: Called asynchronously before an error is emitted.

Streams & buffers::Backpressure.returns: boolean — true when the internal buffer is below highWaterMark after admitting chunk; false when writing should pause until 'drain'.

example.title: Respect writable-stream backpressure
example.explanation: Writes stop as soon as write() reports backpressure and resume only after the drain event.

useCases.title: Throttle a fast producer
useCases.scenario: A producer generates chunks faster than a file, socket, or transform stream can accept them.

useCases.title: Prevent unbounded buffering
useCases.scenario: A loop writes many chunks to a writable stream.

useCases.title: Coordinate producer and consumer
useCases.scenario: A custom pipeline needs to resume only when the downstream writable is ready.

interview.question: What should code do when writable.write() returns false?
interview.answer: write() returns false when the writable stream's internal buffer reaches or exceeds its highWaterMark. The producer should stop writing and wait for drain before sending more chunks.
interview.followUp: What does drain indicate? It indicates that currently buffered chunks have been accepted for delivery by the operating system, so writing can appropriately resume.

interview.question: What does the boolean returned by write() represent?
interview.answer: The return value reports whether the internal buffer remains below the configured highWaterMark after accepting the chunk. A false result signals that further writes should pause until drain.
interview.followUp: Why can ignoring the result be harmful? Continued writes remain buffered while the stream is not draining, increasing queued data instead of matching the consumer's pace.

interview.question: When is the drain event emitted?
interview.answer: The drain event is emitted after all currently buffered chunks are drained, meaning accepted for delivery by the operating system. It is the event that tells paused producer code to continue.
interview.followUp: Should a producer wait for drain after every write? No: wait only after write() returns false; true means the buffer is still below the threshold.

keyPoints: write() returns true while the post-write internal buffer remains below highWaterMark.
A false result applies backpressure: pause the producer immediately.
drain follows delivery of all currently buffered chunks to the operating system.
Listen for drain to determine when writing may appropriately resume.
gotchas: Continuing to call write() during backpressure adds more data to the internal buffer.
Do not resume based on a timer or by repeatedly polling; wait for drain.

Streams & buffers::Object mode.summary: Object mode makes Node.js streams carry JavaScript values instead of being restricted to byte-oriented chunks. Duplex and transform streams can enable it independently on their readable and writable sides.
Streams & buffers::Object mode.explanation: Object mode is enabled when a stream is created with the relevant option. It allows stream operations to carry JavaScript values beyond the normal byte-oriented types. For duplex and transform streams, readableObjectMode and writableObjectMode can configure the two sides independently; on a readable object-mode side, reading yields one value rather than a byte-sized Buffer.

parameters.description: Whether the writable side may accept arbitrary JavaScript values supported by the implementation.

parameters.name: readableObjectMode
parameters.description: Whether the readable side behaves as a stream of objects and returns individual values.

parameters.name: objectMode
parameters.description: Enables object mode for the stream; for duplex streams, the side-specific options provide independent control.

useCases.title: Mixed-mode duplex processing
useCases.scenario: A duplex stream uses different data representations at its input and output boundaries.

interview.question: What does object mode change in a Node.js stream?
interview.answer: Object mode lets a stream accept JavaScript values other than strings, Buffers, TypedArrays, or DataViews, subject to the implementation. A readable object-mode stream returns one value from read() instead of a Buffer sized by the requested byte count.
interview.followUp: How can a transform accept objects but emit bytes? Set writableObjectMode to true and leave the readable side in its default byte-oriented mode.

interview.question: How do you enable object mode?
interview.answer: Set objectMode when constructing the stream. For a Duplex or Transform, readableObjectMode and writableObjectMode let the readable and writable sides be configured independently.
interview.followUp: Why use separate settings? A parser can consume byte chunks on its writable side while emitting parsed records as objects on its readable side.

interview.question: Which values can an object-mode stream carry?
interview.answer: Object mode is not limited to plain object literals; it permits JavaScript values supported by the stream implementation, except null. The normal byte-oriented types remain valid as well.
interview.followUp: What value must never represent an application record? null, because streams use it for a special purpose rather than as ordinary data.

keyPoints: A stream that carries non-byte JavaScript values is operating in object mode.
Enable object mode at stream construction time with the objectMode option.
Writable object mode permits values beyond strings, Buffers, TypedArrays, and DataViews.
Readable object mode returns one value from read(), rather than a Buffer sized by n.
Duplex streams can independently select object mode for readable and writable sides.
The documented default highWaterMark for object-mode streams is 16.
gotchas: Do not use null as an application value: Node.js reserves it for stream control.
For duplex or transform streams, configure readableObjectMode or writableObjectMode when only one side should use object mode.

It accepts the same options as the Readable constructor; object mode is enabled by default, but can be disabled explicitly when the iterable yields stream-compatible byte or string chunks.

parameters.description: An object implementing the Symbol.asyncIterator or Symbol.iterator iterable protocol.

parameters.description: Options accepted by the new stream.Readable([options]) constructor; objectMode defaults to true unless set to false.

interview.question: What does Readable.from() accept and return?

interview.followUp: How can byte-oriented handling be requested? Set the options object's objectMode property to false.

interview.question: What are the parameters of Readable.from()?
interview.answer: The iterable must implement either Symbol.iterator or Symbol.asyncIterator. The options argument contains the options accepted by the Readable constructor.
interview.followUp: What happens when both iteration protocols are available? The method can consume the object as an iterable through the supported protocol; the documentation does not specify precedence.

interview.answer: Object mode defaults to true, so yielded values are treated as objects unless explicitly disabled. A null value is invalid and causes an error event.

interview.question: What does `stream.compose()` return and how does data flow through it?
interview.answer: `stream.compose(...streams)` combines two or more stages into a duplex. Writes go to the first stage, reads come from the last, and intermediate stages are connected with `stream.pipeline`.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from a typical `pipeline` call? A composed duplex remains reusable as a stream value and can itself be piped into another stream, whereas pipeline commonly connects a readable source to a writable destination.

interview.question: What non-stream inputs can compose accept?
interview.answer: A function stage is treated as a factory that receives a source. This lets compose adapt functions, generators, and async iterables into stream stages.
interview.followUp: What contract does an async generator function have? It must accept a source AsyncIterable as its first parameter and cannot yield null.

interview.question: What are the failure semantics of a composed stream?
interview.answer: If any stage errors, Node destroys all supplied stages and the outer duplex. This provides coordinated failure handling across the composition.
interview.followUp: What happens when an async function is used as a stage? It becomes a writable duplex and must resolve to null or undefined.

An async function used as a writable stage must resolve to null or undefined.

interview.question: Why use promise-based `pipeline` instead of manually calling `pipe`?
interview.answer: `pipeline` returns a promise that fulfills when the pipeline completes, and it propagates stream errors through promise rejection. This makes `await pipeline(...)` suitable for structured async error handling.
interview.followUp: What happens to streams on failure? Node calls `destroy(err)` on pipeline streams, with exceptions for streams that already emitted their terminal close or completion events.

interview.question: What does `finished` resolve?
interview.answer: `finished` returns a promise that fulfills once the supplied stream is no longer readable or writable. It is useful when code must wait for a stream's terminal state rather than merely starting an operation.
interview.followUp: How can listener retention be controlled? Pass `cleanup: true` so listeners registered by `finished` are removed before the promise fulfills.

interview.question: How can the `stream/promises` API be imported?
interview.answer: The module can be loaded with `require('node:stream/promises')`; the promise API is also available through `require('node:stream').promises`. Its utilities return promises rather than using callbacks.
interview.followUp: How would cancellation be supplied to `pipeline`? Provide an `AbortSignal` through its options and abort the associated controller when cancellation is required.

interview.question: What are the primary Web Streams types and their roles?
interview.answer: ReadableStream models a source of streaming data, while WritableStream models a destination to which data is sent. TransformStream is the third primary type and applies an algorithm to transform streaming data.
interview.followUp: How can classic Node.js streams interoperate with web streams? Node.js provides toWeb and fromWeb methods on Readable, Writable, and Duplex objects.

interview.question: How can a ReadableStream be consumed asynchronously?
interview.answer: A ReadableStream supports the async iterator protocol, so consumers can process chunks with for await. This provides sequential consumption without manually calling a reader for each chunk.
interview.followUp: What restriction applies while iterating? The stream must not already be locked, and it becomes locked during the iteration.

interview.question: How is data written to a WritableStream?
interview.answer: A WritableStream receives data through a writer obtained with getWriter(). Calling write() sends a chunk to the destination, and close() signals that no more data will be written.
interview.followUp: What does the writer represent? It is the controlled interface used to send chunks to the writable destination.

TransformStream sits between stream endpoints to transform the data passing through.

Synchronous counterparts block the event loop until completion.

interview.question: How do spawn and spawnSync differ?
interview.answer: spawn starts a process asynchronously and returns a ChildProcess immediately, allowing the event loop to continue. spawnSync offers equivalent behavior but blocks until the process exits or is terminated.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid shell parsing for user-controlled arguments? Pass the executable separately from an argument array and do not enable shell execution.

interview.question: What distinguishes exec from spawn?
interview.answer: exec starts a shell, runs the supplied command there, and delivers stdout and stderr to a callback after completion. It is convenient for shell syntax but differs from direct process execution.
interview.followUp: When is spawn preferable? Use it when arguments can be represented separately, especially when avoiding shell interpretation or handling streaming output matters.

interview.question: When should fork be used?
interview.answer: fork is a specialized form of spawn for launching Node.js processes. It returns a ChildProcess and supports the process-to-process communication facilities documented for forked Node.js workers.
interview.followUp: What does fork inherit from the parent? Its Node.js execution arguments are inherited, including relevant Permission Model flags when applicable.

spawn is the general asynchronous primitive and keeps the event loop available while the child runs.
Provide the executable as command and pass its command-line values separately in args; omitted args become an empty array.
fork is intended specifically for starting another Node.js process rather than an arbitrary executable.
The convenience APIs are built on the asynchronous or synchronous spawn primitives.

gotchas: The synchronous APIs block the event loop, so reserve them for situations where blocking is intentional.

System & process::node:cluster.summary: The node:cluster module creates multiple Node.js processes that share server ports, allowing workloads to be distributed among workers. The primary process and workers communicate through IPC, while the application controls worker creation and replacement.
System & process::node:cluster.explanation: The primary process creates workers with cluster.fork(), which uses child processes connected through IPC. Workers can share a server port; the primary normally distributes connections round-robin, while workers may accept connections directly under the alternative scheduling approach. Because workers are separate processes, they can be independently terminated or respawned, but the application must manage the worker count and lifecycle.

interview.question: How does cluster distribute incoming connections?
interview.answer: The primary process owns the listening setup in the default round-robin model, accepts connections, and assigns them to workers. Workers are child processes created with child_process.fork(), and IPC lets them communicate with the primary and exchange server handles.
interview.followUp: How can connection distribution differ? The alternative mode has the primary create the listening socket and pass it to workers, which then accept connections directly.

interview.question: How are workers created and managed?
interview.answer: cluster.fork([env]) creates a worker process and optionally supplies environment-variable overrides. In the primary, worker objects are available through cluster.workers; inside a worker, the current worker is cluster.worker.
interview.followUp: What must the application do after a worker exits? It must listen for lifecycle events and explicitly decide whether and how to fork a replacement, because cluster does not manage the pool automatically.

interview.question: Why choose cluster over worker_threads?
interview.answer: Workers are separate processes, so one can be killed or respawned without directly affecting the others. This provides process isolation, unlike worker_threads, which runs multiple application threads in one Node.js instance.
interview.followUp: When is worker_threads preferable? Use it when process isolation is not needed and threads within one Node.js instance are sufficient.

keyPoints: The module creates multiple Node.js child processes that can listen through the same server port.
Workers are created with child_process.fork(), giving the primary and workers an IPC channel for coordination.
Incoming connections can use either primary-managed round-robin distribution or direct worker acceptance.
The default round-robin scheduler includes logic intended to reduce uneven worker load.
Each worker has process-level isolation, so workers can be independently stopped and started.
Worker objects expose the documented public state and methods for interacting with an individual worker.
gotchas: The module does not maintain a worker pool for you; your application must decide how many workers to create and when to replace them.
Connection distribution is platform-sensitive: round-robin is the default except on Windows, so scheduling behavior should not be assumed to be identical everywhere.
Cluster uses separate processes rather than shared-memory threads; choose worker_threads when process isolation is unnecessary.

System & process::node:worker_threads.explanation: The module creates independent JavaScript execution threads. A main thread starts a Worker, optionally supplies workerData, and communicates through MessagePort objects such as parentPort; values can be transferred or shared using ArrayBuffer and SharedArrayBuffer.

interview.question: When should worker_threads be used?
interview.answer: Worker represents a separate JavaScript execution thread, and most Node.js APIs are available inside it. It is best suited to CPU-intensive JavaScript because asynchronous built-in I/O is more efficient for I/O-bound work.
interview.followUp: How can threads exchange data? They can send messages through MessagePort, transfer ArrayBuffer instances, or share SharedArrayBuffer instances.

interview.question: How does memory sharing differ from transferring data?
interview.answer: Unlike child processes and cluster workers, worker threads can share memory. Sharing uses SharedArrayBuffer, while ArrayBuffer instances can be transferred between threads.
interview.followUp: What communication endpoint does a worker use to talk to its parent? In a worker, parentPort is the MessagePort connected to the parent thread.

interview.question: Which APIs help distinguish and initialize the two execution contexts?
interview.answer: isMainThread indicates whether code is running in the main thread, and workerData contains data supplied when the Worker was created. The worker can send results back through parentPort.
interview.followUp: What does unref() do? It permits the process to exit if that worker is the only active event-system handle.

keyPoints: Importing node:worker_threads gives a Node.js program access to parallel JavaScript execution using threads.
Use workers to move computationally expensive JavaScript away from the main thread.
Worker threads provide shared-memory capabilities that distinguish them from process-based concurrency APIs.
Communication can move ArrayBuffer ownership or expose shared state through SharedArrayBuffer.
Each Worker instance is an independent JavaScript execution context with its own thread.
Inside worker code, parentPort is the MessagePort used to communicate with the spawning thread.
Environment data configured by the parent is cloned for each newly created worker.
gotchas: Workers are intended for CPU-heavy JavaScript, not ordinary I/O-heavy tasks; Node's asynchronous I/O is generally more efficient.
Calling unref() changes process-liveness behavior: the worker no longer keeps the event loop alive when it is the only active handle.

interview.question: What is `process.exitCode`?
interview.answer: It is the exit status Node.js uses when the process exits gracefully. Setting it does not immediately terminate the process; Node exits when no additional event-loop work remains.
interview.followUp: What happens if `process.exit()` is called without a code after setting it? It uses the previously set `process.exitCode` value.

interview.question: What values can `process.exitCode` contain?
interview.answer: Its documented type is integer, string, null, or undefined, and its default is undefined. String values are restricted to integer strings.
interview.followUp: What status does Node normally use when no asynchronous operations remain and no exit code was set? It normally exits with status 0.

interview.question: How does it differ from `process.exit()`?
interview.answer: Assigning `process.exitCode` lets the process finish naturally, so pending event-loop work can complete. Calling `process.exit()` instead requests synchronous termination with an exit status.
interview.followUp: Why can explicit termination be risky for output? Synchronous termination can occur before pending writes complete, whereas natural exit waits for the event loop to drain.

Update it through direct assignment when application logic determines the final status.
An explicit `process.exit(code)` call can also establish the value, although it terminates synchronously.
If no nonzero status is selected, Node normally reports success once asynchronous work is complete.
gotchas: String values must contain integers; arbitrary text is not a valid exit code.
Do not use `process.exit()` merely to select a status when graceful shutdown is desired, because it terminates synchronously.

interview.question: How do you handle SIGINT and SIGTERM in Node.js?
interview.answer: Node.js emits signal events when the process receives signals, and the handler receives the signal name as its first argument. Register listeners with process.on(), commonly for SIGINT and SIGTERM.
interview.followUp: What changes after installing one of these listeners? The corresponding default behavior is removed, so the application must perform its own cleanup and termination.

interview.question: How would you begin a graceful server shutdown?
interview.answer: Call the server's close operation from the signal handler to stop accepting new work, then exit after its completion callback indicates shutdown has finished. Cleanup should also account for resources besides the server.
interview.followUp: How would you prevent shutdown from hanging? Add an application-level deadline and force termination if cleanup does not complete in time.

interview.question: What are the platform differences between SIGINT and SIGTERM?
interview.answer: SIGINT is commonly produced by Ctrl+C and is supported on all platforms. SIGTERM has default handlers on non-Windows platforms, but Windows does not support it as a delivered signal.
interview.followUp: Why should portable code still register both? They represent different shutdown paths: interactive interruption and termination requested by a process manager.

A shared callback can distinguish the shutdown cause from its first argument.
Ctrl+C is the usual interactive way to produce SIGINT.
Without custom listeners, these signals have built-in non-Windows handling.

interview.answer: autocannon is an HTTP/1.1 benchmarking tool for Node.js. It supports HTTP pipelining and HTTPS, and can be used through its command-line interface or API.

interview.answer: The API signature is `autocannon(opts[, cb])`. The required `url` identifies the HTTP or HTTPS target, while `connections` controls concurrent connections and defaults to 10.

interview.question: How does autocannon decide when to stop?

interview.followUp: Why does `sampleInt` matter? It determines the interval between samples, which affects the number of samples and therefore statistical analysis.

interview.question: Why is MSW less coupled to the HTTP client than many mocking libraries?
interview.answer: MSW intercepts requests at the network layer rather than patching a specific request library. This keeps the tested application code unchanged and allows the same handlers to work with different HTTP clients.
interview.followUp: How does Node.js interception differ from browser interception? In the browser MSW uses a Service Worker; in Node.js it uses request interception implemented without module patching.

interview.question: What can a request handler do after matching a request?
interview.answer: Handlers describe how intercepted requests should be handled. They can return a mocked Response, pass the request through, or return nothing so MSW can continue looking for another matching handler.
interview.followUp: What happens when several handlers match? MSW evaluates them in order, and only the handler that becomes responsible for handling the request determines the result.

interview.question: How are the same handlers shared between tests and the browser?
interview.answer: Use setupServer(...handlers) for a Node.js process and setupWorker(...handlers) for a browser process. Start the selected runtime with server.listen() or worker.start() to enable interception.
interview.followUp: How can a test isolate a temporary behavior? Add an override with .use(), then call .resetHandlers() during cleanup to remove runtime handlers.

interview.question: How does Nock prevent a test from reaching the network?
interview.answer: Nock intercepts Node HTTP traffic by overriding `http.request` and also `http.ClientRequest`. Tests define interceptors for the expected request and receive the configured reply instead of contacting the remote server.
interview.followUp: How would you diagnose an unexpected real request? Check that Nock is active, that the interceptor matches the request exactly, and that the module did not capture an HTTP import before Nock loaded.

interview.question: How do you declare and verify an expected request?
interview.answer: An interceptor is created from a scope such as `nock("https://example.test")`, followed by an HTTP method like `.get(path)` and a response such as `.reply(status, body)`. Matching includes the request target and method, with request-body matching available for methods such as GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE.
interview.followUp: How can a test verify that every declared request was made? Inspect the interceptor state with `nock.isDone()` or the scope's completion expectations after the operation under test.

interview.question: What is the difference between `restore`, `activate`, and `isActive`?
interview.answer: `nock.restore()` returns HTTP behavior to its normal unmocked state and removes Nock's interceptor. If interception is needed again, call `nock.activate()`; `nock.isActive()` reports whether the interceptor is active.
interview.followUp: How can tests intentionally use real services? Set `NOCK_OFF=true`, which bypasses Nock so HTTP calls reach the actual servers.

Calling `nock.restore()` removes the interceptor, so later tests need `nock.activate()` before requests can be intercepted.
Setting `NOCK_OFF=true` deliberately bypasses mocks and sends tests to real servers; use it only when that behavior is intended.

interview.answer: `node:test` is Node.js’s built-in module for creating JavaScript tests, so it does not require an external test-runner dependency. Tests can be run with the `node --test` command.
interview.followUp: How would you run tests continuously? Use the runner’s watch mode with `node --test --watch`.

interview.question: How do `test()` and `describe()` differ?
interview.answer: `test()` registers an individual test, while `describe()` groups related tests into a suite. The callback receives a `TestContext`, which supports operations such as skipping tests, adding diagnostics, and creating subtests.
interview.followUp: What does a completed `test()` call produce? It returns a promise that fulfills after the test completes.

interview.question: What built-in testing capabilities does the runner provide?

interview.question: What problem does SuperTest solve?
interview.answer: SuperTest provides a high-level API for testing HTTP servers and is built on SuperAgent. Passing an application lets it create and manage a server for the request, while chained expectations validate the response.

interview.question: What kinds of response checks can it perform?

interview.question: How does Commander generate and display help?
interview.answer: Help is generated from the commands, options, and arguments already configured. The default help option is `-h,--help`; `.help()` exits after displaying help, while `.outputHelp()` displays it without exiting.

interview.question: What does dotenv.config() do?
interview.answer: dotenv.config() reads and parses the .env file, writes its values to process.env, and returns an object containing parsed content or an error. The package therefore provides both environment setup and a result that can be inspected.
interview.followUp: How can variables be loaded before application code without an explicit call? Import dotenv/config before those modules, or preload dotenv through Node's module-loading option.

interview.question: Why should dotenv be loaded early?
interview.answer: The documentation recommends importing and configuring dotenv as early as possible. This matters because imported modules may read process.env while they initialize, before later application code runs.

interview.question: What does cron.schedule do?
interview.answer: schedule(expression, func, options?) creates a task and starts it immediately. The expression is a valid cron string, the function is the work to run, and options are optional execution settings.
interview.followUp: How would you delay startup? Use createTask instead, attach listeners or inspect the task, and call start() explicitly.

interview.question: Which cron expressions does node-cron support?
interview.answer: node-cron accepts five or six cron fields. The optional first field is seconds; with five fields, seconds default to zero, while fields also support ranges, steps, and comma-separated lists.
interview.followUp: How would you run every 30 seconds? Use the six-field expression */30 * * * * *.

interview.question: Which options help control execution behavior?
interview.answer: Set timezone to an IANA name such as UTC or Europe/London when the schedule must be evaluated in a particular zone. Set noOverlap to true when a later invocation must be skipped while the prior execution remains active.
interview.followUp: How can a fleet avoid duplicate work? Enable distributed, provide name, and use the configured run coordinator.

interview.question: How do you send an email through SMTP?
interview.answer: Create a transporter with nodemailer.createTransport(), configure its SMTP host, port, security, and authentication, then call transporter.sendMail() with the message. Nodemailer supports either a configuration object or a connection URL.
interview.followUp: How would you improve throughput for many messages? Enable pool: true, reuse one transporter, and tune maxConnections and maxMessages.

interview.question: How does SMTP connection pooling work?
interview.answer: Set pool to true to reuse SMTP connections across messages. maxConnections limits simultaneous connections, while maxMessages controls how many messages use one connection before it is reopened.
interview.followUp: What happens when every pooled connection is busy? New messages are queued until a connection becomes available.

interview.question: How are attachments added?
interview.answer: Put attachment objects in the message's attachments array. An attachment can provide content directly or reference a file path, URL, data URI, or readable stream; filename controls the recipient-visible name.
interview.followUp: How should large attachments be handled? Prefer path, href, or a readable stream so data is streamed instead of fully loaded into memory.

Utilities & tooling::pm2.explanation: PM2 runs Node.js applications under supervision, restarting them after crashes or machine restarts. Its cluster mode distributes a networked application across CPUs, while reload replaces workers one at a time; PM2 also centralizes logs and can rotate them through its pm2-logrotate module.

pm2 start api.js -i max
pm2 reload all
pm2 logs api
pm2 install pm2-logrotate
example.explanation: Starts the API across available CPUs, reloads workers without downtime, streams its logs, and installs automatic log rotation.

useCases.title: Scale a network server
useCases.scenario: Deploy an HTTP API across all available CPU cores.

useCases.title: Perform zero-downtime updates
useCases.scenario: Release application updates while retaining service availability.

useCases.scenario: Keep services running through crashes and host reboots.

interview.question: How does PM2 cluster mode improve availability and CPU utilization?
interview.answer: Cluster mode starts multiple child processes that share the server port, allowing a networked Node.js application to use available CPUs. PM2 provides the built-in load balancer, so the application does not need code changes for this scaling model.
interview.followUp: What happens during a reload? PM2 replaces processes one at a time and keeps at least one process running; an unsuccessful reload can time out and fall back to a classic restart.

interview.question: What is the difference between PM2 restart and reload?
interview.answer: `restart` stops and starts all processes together, creating a short unavailable period. `reload` restarts processes sequentially while retaining at least one running process, which supports zero-downtime updates.
interview.followUp: What application-side behavior is required? The app must shut down gracefully, finish remaining requests, and close external connections.

interview.question: How does PM2 handle logs and log rotation?
interview.answer: PM2 stores application logs under `~/.pm2/logs` and exposes them with `pm2 logs`. For automatic rotation, install the `pm2-logrotate` module.
interview.followUp: How can clustered output be consolidated? Configure `merge_logs: true` in the ecosystem file to combine instance logs into one output and one error file.

Application output is collected under `~/.pm2/logs` and can be viewed live with the logs command.

gotchas: Use reload rather than restart for service updates when a brief outage is unacceptable, because restart stops every process simultaneously.
A reload can fall back to a normal restart after a timeout, so the application must start and become ready reliably.
Implement graceful shutdown so in-flight requests finish and external connections close before a worker exits.

interview.question: What is sharp and why is it fast?
interview.answer: sharp is a Node-API image-processing module powered by libvips. It is designed for common transformations such as resizing and conversion to JPEG, PNG, WebP, GIF, or AVIF, and it processes small regions to reduce memory use.
interview.followUp: How can a pipeline avoid enlarging small images? Use resize with withoutEnlargement: true, accepting that the resulting dimensions may be smaller than the requested target.

interview.question: How does sharp resize images?
interview.answer: resize accepts optional width, height, and options, and returns the Sharp instance so operations can be chained. With both dimensions, fit controls whether the image is cropped, letterboxed, stretched, or constrained inside or outside the target.
interview.followUp: What is the default fit behavior? cover preserves aspect ratio and crops or clips as needed to cover both dimensions.

interview.question: Which formats and I/O mechanisms does sharp support?
interview.answer: The module can read JPEG, PNG, WebP, GIF, AVIF, TIFF, and SVG, and can emit common encoded formats including JPEG, PNG, WebP, GIF, AVIF, and TIFF, plus raw pixels. Input and output can use files, buffers, or streams.
interview.followUp: How is output format selected when no format method is used? For file output, sharp infers it from the filename extension.

Memory use is reduced by working on small portions of uncompressed image data rather than retaining the whole image.

The resize operation can set width, height, or both dimensions.
gotchas: Using withoutEnlargement can produce dimensions below the requested target when the source is already smaller.
When no encoder is chosen explicitly, the destination filename extension determines the output format.

interview.question: How does Socket.IO differ from plain WebSockets?
interview.answer:
question: How does Socket.IO differ from plain WebSockets?
answer: It adds automatic reconnection, packet buffering, acknowledgements, room-based broadcasting, connection state recovery, and namespaces. The underlying Engine.IO layer can use HTTP long-polling when WebSocket is unavailable.
followUp: How is a dead connection detected?
answer: The server periodically sends PING packets, and the client must answer with PONG within the configured timeout; failure causes the connection to be considered closed.
interview.followUp: How is a dead connection detected? The server periodically sends PING packets, and the client must answer with PONG within the configured timeout; failure causes the connection to be considered closed.

interview.question: What is a room and what is it used for?
interview.answer:
Rooms are arbitrary channels that sockets can join or leave. The server can emit to a room to target only its members, while a socket can also leave explicitly.

Follow-up: What happens to rooms during disconnection? The socket leaves its rooms automatically.
interview.followUp: What happens to rooms during disconnection? The socket leaves its rooms automatically.

interview.question: How do acknowledgements work?
interview.answer:
An acknowledgement is a request-response pattern layered on an event. A callback can be supplied as the last emit argument, or emitWithAck() can return a Promise that resolves after the other side responds.

Follow-up: What limitation applies to older server APIs? Older documentation states that acknowledgements are not supported when broadcasting; current 4.x documentation adds broadcast acknowledgements from version 4.5.0.
interview.followUp: What limitation applies to older server APIs? Older documentation states that acknowledgements are not supported when broadcasting; current 4.x documentation adds broadcast acknowledgements from version 4.5.0.

keyPoints: Transport reliability improves because HTTP long-polling is available when WebSocket setup fails.
Emissions can target every connected client or only members of a room.
The current API includes connection-state recovery for temporary interruptions.

Use Pool when one origin needs several connections, Client for one connection, and MockAgent to intercept requests during testing; interceptors can add cross-cutting behavior through dispatcher composition.

interview.question: What is the difference between Pool and Client?
interview.answer: Pool manages a fixed set of connections to one origin, while Client maps to one TCP connection. Use Pool when multiple connections to the same origin are useful and Client when single-connection control is needed.
interview.followUp: How would requests reach a custom Pool? Pass that Pool as the request's dispatcher option, allowing the request to use the Pool's connection management.

interview.question: How can Undici requests be mocked?
interview.answer: MockAgent is a dispatcher for replacing network behavior with configured responses. Create one, install it with setGlobalDispatcher, obtain a mock pool for an origin, and register an intercept before making the request.
interview.followUp: What is the role of the origin-specific object returned by get? It scopes interception rules to the selected origin, such as https://api.example.com.

interview.question: What are Undici interceptors used for?
interview.answer: Interceptors are composable dispatch behavior that adds cross-cutting features such as retries, decompression, redirects, or DNS caching. They can be applied to a Client or Pool with dispatcher.compose().
interview.followUp: Does interceptor order matter? Yes: interceptors are applied in compose order, with the first array element forming the outermost layer.

keyPoints: Dispatchers centralize connection management for request APIs.
Use Pool to control several connections for a single origin.
Client is the low-level choice for one connection.
Choose Agent when requests must be routed across multiple origins.
gotchas: Client does not pipeline requests unless pipelining is explicitly configured.
Do not assume invocation order determines dispatch order.
Enable Client pipelining only when the remote server is trusted.

Utilities & tooling::winston.summary: Winston is a Node.js logging library that sends records to multiple transports. It combines formats, severity levels, and per-transport maximum levels to control how and where logs are emitted.

A logger-level format establishes common record formatting, while transports can also be configured independently; formats are composed as an ordered pipeline and may transform or discard records.

interview.question: What is a Winston transport?
interview.answer: A transport is a destination for log records, such as the console or a file. One logger can use several transports, allowing different destinations to receive different subsets of messages.
interview.followUp: How would you route failures separately from routine logs? Add an error-level file transport alongside a general console transport, giving each transport its own level.

interview.question: How do logger and transport levels interact?
interview.answer: The logger's level controls which messages enter logging, while a transport's level specifies the maximum level that transport records. Because transports are independent, each can filter the same logger stream differently.
interview.followUp: What happens if the logger level is more restrictive than a transport level? Messages rejected by the logger do not reach any transport, regardless of that transport's setting.

interview.question: How does Winston formatting work?
interview.answer: Formats are available through winston.format and are composed with format.combine. A format can alter the info record or produce its output representation, and the combined formats run in array order.
interview.followUp: Why should a mutating format precede JSON output? A later output format may serialize the record before a subsequent mutation can affect the emitted representation.

The transports option supplies the destinations that handle log records.

interview.question: How does yargs structure subcommands?
interview.answer: A command is registered with command(), which can specify its name, description, builder, and handler. The builder describes command-specific arguments, while the handler receives the parsed argv when that command runs.
interview.followUp: How would you add typed positional values? Use positional() inside the command builder, giving each positional key parsing options such as type and description.

interview.question: How does yargs middleware work?
interview.answer: Middleware is registered with middleware() and may be a function or an array of functions. Each callback receives argv, and middleware executes in list order for commands.
interview.followUp: When should middleware run before validation? Pass true as the second argument so it executes after parsing but before validation checks.

interview.question: What does yargs validation provide?

interview.question: What does a Zod schema do at runtime?
interview.answer: Zod lets you define schemas for primitive values and nested objects, then validate data against those schemas. A valid parse returns a strongly typed deep clone; an invalid parse throws ZodError.

useCases.scenario: Keep route contracts close to handlers using declarative JSON Schema definitions.

interview.question: Which components perform validation and serialization?
interview.answer: Fastify uses Ajv v8 for request validation and fast-json-stringify for response-body serialization. Schemas are declared in the route options, and response serialization is enabled when an output schema is present.
interview.followUp: What inputs can a route schema validate? It can cover the body, query string, route parameters, and request headers.

interview.question: How do you validate a request in Fastify?
interview.answer: Add JSON Schema under the route's schema option, using fields such as body, querystring or query, params, headers, and response. The validator checks incoming data before the handler proceeds.
interview.followUp: What happens when validation fails? Fastify returns a validation error instead of invoking the route handler.

interview.question: What is the purpose of a response schema?
interview.answer: A response schema describes the output shape and lets fast-json-stringify generate JSON efficiently. It can also help avoid accidentally exposing fields that are not part of the declared response shape.
interview.followUp: Why declare response schemas even when validation is not needed? They can improve serialization throughput and constrain the serialized output.

keyPoints: Routes can define behavior through schemas rather than relying only on imperative checks.
JSON Schema is the recommended format for both input validation and output serialization.
Fastify separates request validation from response serialization, and both mechanisms can be customized.
Ajv v8 checks incoming route data against the declared JSON Schema.
fast-json-stringify handles JSON response serialization when the route declares an output schema.
Request validation is configured by placing the desired constraints in the route schema.

Web frameworks::h3.summary: H3 is a lightweight, composable server framework for modern JavaScript runtimes. It uses web-standard primitives and a small core that can be extended with handlers, middleware, and tree-shakable utilities.
Web frameworks::h3.explanation: H3 provides a small application core that works with web-standard request and response primitives. Create an H3 instance, register handlers or middleware, and compose applications or utilities around it; returned handler values are converted into web responses.
Web frameworks::h3.returns: An H3 application instance whose registered handlers process requests and produce web responses.

example.explanation: Creates an H3 application and registers a GET route that returns a response-compatible value.

useCases.title: Cross-runtime web servers
useCases.scenario: Build a small HTTP service with standard Web APIs and minimal framework overhead.

useCases.title: Global request middleware
useCases.scenario: Add authentication, logging, or error interception around every request.

useCases.title: Composable server architecture
useCases.scenario: Combine an H3 application with compatible web handlers or nested applications.

interview.question: What is H3 and what design principles does it follow?
interview.answer: H3 is a lightweight, composable server framework for modern JavaScript runtimes. It uses web-standard primitives such as Request, Response, URL, and Headers, which helps it work across compatible runtimes.
interview.followUp: How does H3 remain extensible? Start with a lightweight H3 instance, then add built-in tree-shakable utilities or your own functionality.

interview.question: How are routes registered and selected in H3?
interview.answer: Instantiate H3 with `new H3()`, then register handlers through methods such as `on`, method shortcuts, or `all`. Each request is matched to one most-specific route handler.
interview.followUp: What distinguishes a route pattern from a URL? It is a pathname, with rou3 syntax, rather than a complete URL.

interview.question: How does middleware work in H3?
interview.answer: Global middleware is registered with `H3.use` and runs on every request before the route handler. Middleware can wrap the next middleware or handler, allowing it to intercept requests, responses, and errors.
interview.followUp: When would route middleware be preferable? Use it when protection should apply only to a particular route or route pattern.

keyPoints: Its core model is built around standard Web API request, response, URL, and header objects.
H3 can host compatible handlers and integrate with supported runtimes without requiring a runtime-specific programming model.
Functionality is added incrementally through utilities or application code, helping avoid an unnecessarily large core.
gotchas: Enabling debug mode can expose stack traces, so it should not be enabled in production.

Web frameworks::hono.summary: Hono is a small web framework built on Web Standards such as Fetch, allowing the same application code to run across runtimes including Node.js, Bun, Deno, and edge platforms. Node.js uses an adapter to serve the standard handler.
Web frameworks::hono.explanation: Hono builds applications around Web-standard request and response APIs, so the application code can remain the same across supported runtimes. Runtime-specific entry points or adapters connect that shared handler to environments such as Node.js, Bun, Deno, and edge platforms.
Web frameworks::hono.syntax:
const app = new Hono()
app.get('/', (c) => c.text('Hello World'))
Web frameworks::hono.returns: A Fetch-compatible Hono application handler; the runtime-specific adapter or platform entry point serves it.

example.title: Run a Hono app on Node.js
example.code:
import { Hono } from 'hono'
import { serve } from '@hono/node-server'

const app = new Hono()

app.get('/', (c) => c.text('Hello World'))

serve({ fetch: app.fetch, port: 3000 })
example.explanation: Creates a Hono app with a standard Fetch-style handler, then runs it through the Node.js adapter.

useCases.title: Multi-runtime services
useCases.scenario: Build one HTTP application for multiple deployment targets without rewriting its core routes.

useCases.title: Native Fetch runtimes
useCases.scenario: Deploy a Hono Fetch handler to Bun or Deno, where the runtime serves it natively.

useCases.title: Node.js applications
useCases.scenario: Run the same standard-based application on Node.js through the Node adapter.

useCases.title: Platform-specific capabilities
useCases.scenario: Use a separate integration package when application features depend on a platform.

interview.question: Why is Hono portable across runtimes?
interview.answer: Hono uses Web-standard APIs such as Fetch, Request, Response, URL, URLSearchParams, and Headers. Because supported runtimes implement these standards, the application code can run across multiple platforms.
interview.followUp: How does Hono support Node.js if Node.js is not a native Fetch-handler platform in the same way as Bun or Deno? It uses a Node.js adapter to connect the standard handler to Node.js.

interview.question: What changes when the same Hono app is deployed to another runtime?
interview.answer: The core application code is shared, while the runtime-specific entry point can differ. For Node.js, the Node adapter serves the Hono Fetch handler; other runtimes can provide their own entry-point integration.
interview.followUp: What should be isolated when moving an app between runtimes? Keep platform-dependent capabilities behind the relevant adapter rather than embedding them in portable application code.

interview.question: Which runtimes can Hono target?
interview.answer: Hono supports Cloudflare Workers, Deno, Bun, Fastly Compute, AWS Lambda, Node.js, Vercel edge functions, and WebAssembly with WASI HTTP support, among others. The common Web Standards foundation enables the shared code model.
interview.followUp: Does portability mean every capability behaves identically everywhere? No; platform-specific functions can need separate adapters and runtime-specific setup.

keyPoints: Hono centers its API on Web Standards, including Fetch-style HTTP primitives rather than runtime-specific server APIs.
Application logic can be reused across supported platforms, with runtime-specific setup kept at the entry point.
Node.js integration is provided through a dedicated adapter that connects Hono to the Node runtime.

Web frameworks::koa.sourceTitle: Koa - next generation web framework for node.js
Web frameworks::koa.summary: Koa is a Node.js web framework built around async middleware and a unified request/response context. Its core omits bundled middleware, keeping routing and other features modular.
Web frameworks::koa.explanation: Koa builds applications from async middleware. Each middleware receives a single context object containing request and response helpers plus a next function for composing downstream middleware; Koa's async model lets errors propagate without callback-based control flow.

parameters.description: The Koa middleware function, typically an async function receiving the current context and downstream middleware callback.

parameters.name: ctx
parameters.description: The current request/response context, exposed to middleware as `ctx`.

parameters.name: next
parameters.description: Function that invokes downstream middleware when awaited.

Web frameworks::koa.returns: A Koa application instance from which middleware can be registered and an HTTP server can be started.

interview.question: How does Koa middleware composition work?
interview.answer: Koa middleware is an async function that receives `ctx` and `next`. Awaiting `next()` transfers control to downstream middleware and then resumes the current function during the upstream phase.
interview.followUp: What happens if middleware does not await `next()`? Downstream execution is not composed into the current middleware's flow, so later behavior may be skipped or reordered.

interview.question: What is `ctx` in Koa?
interview.answer: `ctx` is Koa's per-request context and exposes request and response-related functionality through one object. Middleware uses it to read input and produce the response, commonly by assigning `ctx.body`.
interview.followUp: Why avoid direct use of `ctx.res`? Koa documents bypassing its response handling as unsupported and warns against using raw Node response methods.

interview.question: What distinguishes Koa from a bundled web framework?
interview.answer: Koa uses async functions to avoid callback-style middleware and improve error handling. Its core remains small because middleware is not bundled into the framework.
interview.followUp: How would an application add routing? Select and install a separate Koa-compatible routing middleware rather than expecting routing in Koa core.

keyPoints: Middleware is written with async functions, so control flow does not require nested callback conventions.
The async model is intended to make application error handling substantially easier.
Register middleware with `app.use`; the middleware receives the request context and a downstream function.
Koa exposes the active middleware context through the application’s current-context mechanism when configured for it.
The raw Node response is available as `ctx.res`, but application code should normally use Koa's response interface.
gotchas: Plan to add required capabilities, such as routing or parsing, through separate middleware packages.
Use Koa's response APIs instead of directly manipulating the underlying Node response object.

Web frameworks::polka.sourceTitle: lukeed/polka: A micro web server so fast, it'll make you smile :)
Web frameworks::polka.summary: Polka is a minimal, high-performance Express alternative built on Node's native HTTP server. It adds routing, middleware, and sub-application support with a similar application and route API.
Web frameworks::polka.explanation: Polka creates a native Node.js HTTP server with routing, middleware, and sub-application support. Routes use HTTP methods and path patterns, while middleware receives the request, response, and a next callback; the application handler can also be passed to a custom server.
Web frameworks::polka.syntax:
polka(opts?)
app.METHOD(pattern, handler)
app.use(pattern?, ...handlers)
app.listen(port, callback?)

parameters.description: Optional configuration object for the Polka application.

parameters.description: Function executed for a matching route.

parameters.name: req
parameters.description: Incoming request passed to middleware or handlers.

parameters.name: res
parameters.description: Outgoing response passed to middleware or handlers.

parameters.name: next
parameters.description: Callback that continues middleware processing.

interview.question: What is Polka?
interview.answer: Polka is a minimal Express alternative built around Node's native HTTP server. It adds routing, middleware, and sub-application support while keeping a similar application and route API.
interview.followUp: How can Polka work with another HTTP server? Pass the application's `handler` function to that server, as shown by the documentation's custom-server pattern.

interview.question: How are routes defined?
interview.answer: A route is declared with `app.METHOD(pattern, handler)`. The method is a lowercased valid HTTP method, the pattern is a routing string, and the handler runs when the request matches.
interview.followUp: Can the same path be used for multiple methods? Yes; a pathname or pattern may be reused with different methods.

interview.question: How does middleware execution work?
interview.answer: Middleware runs between receiving a request and executing the matched route handler. Its signature is `(req, res, next)`, and calling `next()` continues the chain.
interview.followUp: What happens when middleware ends the response? The chain exits early and the route handler does not run, regardless of the response status code.

keyPoints: Polka targets applications that want an Express-like interface with a smaller implementation.
Its core is Node's native HTTP server augmented with routing, middleware, and mounted sub-applications.
The application and route-pattern APIs closely resemble Express conventions.
Every route combines a path pattern, an HTTP method, and the function that handles a match.
Middleware receives the request and response objects plus a callback for advancing execution.
Middleware is organized in tiers, allowing application-level and route-related processing before handlers.
gotchas: An error in middleware stops the remaining middleware and prevents the route handler from running.
Ending a response early likewise stops the middleware chain and route execution, regardless of status code.

Web frameworks::restify.summary: Restify is a Node.js web-service framework optimized for semantically correct RESTful services. Its plugin API includes token-bucket throttling by IP, forwarded IP, or username, plus an inflight-request limit.
Web frameworks::restify.explanation: Restify provides a Node.js server framework for semantically correct RESTful services. Its request pipeline accepts middleware such as the built-in throttle plugin, which applies global rate and burst limits and can select IP, forwarded IP, or username as the throttling key; exhausted clients receive HTTP 429.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Required options object containing `burst`, `rate`, and optional identity and header settings.

Web frameworks::restify.returns: The throttle middleware returns an HTTP 429 response when a client has exhausted its available rate or burst; otherwise request processing continues.

interview.question: How does Restify’s throttling middleware work?
interview.answer: The throttle plugin is a token-bucket rate limiter that plugs into Restify’s normal request pipeline. Configure global `rate` and `burst` values, then optionally choose IP, X-Forwarded-For, or username keys.
interview.followUp: How does a client-specific policy work? Set blanket top-level limits and provide an `overrides` object containing rates for selected users or IPs.

interview.question: What do the throttle plugin’s rate and burst options represent?
interview.answer: `rate` and `burst` are request rates expressed per second. `burst` permits short-term capacity above the sustained rate, while `rate` controls replenishment.
interview.followUp: What response should callers handle when capacity is exhausted? They should handle HTTP 429 Too Many Requests and retry according to their client policy.

interview.question: Which identities can Restify throttle?
interview.answer: The plugin can throttle by username, IP address, or X-Forwarded-For. Username-based throttling uses `req.username`, while IP/XFF uses address matching.
interview.followUp: When would forwarded-address throttling need special care? It should only be enabled when the deployment’s proxy and trust model make the forwarded value reliable.

keyPoints: The throttle plugin integrates into the standard Restify request-handling pipeline.
Its limiter uses a token-bucket model rather than only rejecting requests at fixed intervals.
Throttling can use the client IP, forwarded IP, or username from `req.username`.
Global limits can be supplemented with per-key overrides for selected clients.
Both limits accept integer or floating-point request-per-second values.
A separate inflight-request throttle caps how many requests the server handles concurrently.
gotchas: Clients that exhaust their configured rate or burst receive HTTP 429.
IP and X-Forwarded-For throttling uses a /32 match, so address handling can affect client grouping.
